meta.subtitle: Integrated energy major and a net debtor; 2026 estimates lifted by refining and gas strength, with the shares near their 52-week high

analystCommentary: We rate ExxonMobil **HOLD** with a target range of $140 to $163. Consensus expects FY26E EPS of $11.80, far above FY25's $6.70, then $10.84 in FY27E. The 10-Q frames 2026 around supply disruptions in the Middle East and refining capacity reductions, though it also places average crude prices within their 10-year range. At $161.23 the shares sit near the top of their $110.39–$176.41 52-week range. Our Base values FY27E a year out at the multiple the market pays for that estimate today, so it returns roughly today's price. The Bull adds a modest gain if the 2026 conditions last, and the Bear takes the shares back to their 52-week low if they unwind. The weighted value sits a little below the price and the page derives HOLD; the Scenarios section argues the input the label turns on. The balance sheet gives less support than the earnings suggest: ExxonMobil ended FY25 with net debt of $32.9B, up from $18.7B, after dividends and buybacks together ran ahead of free cash flow of $23.6B.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas and manufactures fuels, chemicals and specialty products. The company description names four segments, Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products and Specialty Products, and the company sells under the Exxon, Esso and Mobil brands. It was founded in 1870, is headquartered in Spring, Texas, and changed its name from Exxon Mobil Corporation to ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation in July 2026; the pack does not describe the corporate structure behind the rename. The revenue data in the pack carry only a consolidated total, so this report does not split revenue by business line. FY25 revenue was $332.2B ({- -5.0% -}), net income was $28.8B and diluted EPS was $6.70. The shares trade at $161.23 for a market capitalization of ~$663B on 4.11B shares, with a dividend yield of 2.60%.

thesis.body: Our thesis is that the 2026 earnings step-up is real but partly cyclical, and that today's price already pays for the consensus view of it. The 10-Q, filed in August 2026, describes a second quarter with supply disruptions in the Middle East, global industry refining margins sharply above their 10-year historical range and natural gas prices above their 10-year average, while chemical margins stayed below the bottom of theirs. It also places average crude oil prices within their 10-year range, so the conditions it puts out of range are refining and gas, not crude. The pack has no breakdown of earnings by driver, so we cannot say how much of the step-up those conditions produced; some of the gain may last and some may unwind. With the shares near their 52-week high, we see a modest reward if the conditions last against a larger loss if they reverse, which leaves the shares fairly valued rather than cheap or expensive.

catalysts: A longer disruption: if the refining and gas conditions last through 2027, consensus would likely lift FY27E toward the FY26E level; the Bull case prices that.
Advantaged-asset growth in Permian, Guyana and LNG, plus the integrated benefits the company plans from Denbury and Pioneer; see Growth.
Structural cost savings measured against 2019, which support earnings through the cycle; the Business and moat section carries the figures.
risks: Faster normalization: the refining and gas strength could fade sooner than consensus models; the Bear case prices a full unwind.
Commodity exposure in both directions, as the 10-K risk factors set out; see Risks.
A net debtor paying out more than its free cash flow; the Capital allocation section carries the detail.
Energy transition and long-run demand risk; the Risks section covers the systemic exposures.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue peaked at $413.7B in FY22 and drifted lower over the next three years: $344.6B in FY23 ({- -16.7% -}), $349.6B in FY24 ({+ +1.5% +}) and $332.2B in FY25 ({- -5.0% -}). Net income fell from $55.7B in FY22 to $28.8B in FY25, and diluted EPS from $13.26 to $6.70. The trend broke in 2026: Q2'26 revenue was $116B, {+ +42.3% +} year over year, in the market conditions the thesis describes. The pack carries no operating-income or EBITDA line for ExxonMobil, so we read profitability through net income; the trailing-twelve-month net margin is 8.9%. Consensus sees FY26E revenue of ~$411B and EPS of $11.80, then EPS of $10.84 in FY27E. Both EPS estimates sit above every year from FY23 to FY25, so consensus expects most of the 2026 strength to carry into FY27E. Whether it does is the question the scenarios weigh.
financials.balanceCommentary: ExxonMobil is a net debtor. At FY25 year-end total debt was $43.5B against cash and short-term investments of $10.7B, for net debt of $32.9B. Debt itself has moved little over five years: $47.7B in FY21 and between $41.2B and $41.7B in FY22 through FY24, before the small FY25 rise. The swing in net debt has come from cash. Cash built to $31.5B in FY23, which brought net debt down to $10.0B, then fell to $23.0B in FY24 and to the FY25 level above, so net debt rose to $18.7B in FY24 and rose sharply again in FY25, back toward the $40.9B of FY21. Against the company's size the load is moderate: FY25 net debt is a small fraction of total equity of $266.6B and less than one year of FY25 operating cash flow. The pack has no EBITDA line, so net debt/EBITDA and interest coverage are blank, and we do not estimate them. Liquidity is adequate rather than ample: the current ratio was 1.15 at FY25 and 1.13 on a trailing basis, down from 1.48 in FY23. The pack has no mid-2026 balance sheet, so the year-end figures are the latest we have. The direction matters more than the level, and the drawdown behind it is a capital-allocation choice that the Management section discusses.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was $52.0B in FY25, down from $76.8B in FY22 and $55.0B in FY24. Capital expenditure rose every year, from $12.1B in FY21 to $28.4B in FY25, so free cash flow fell from $58.4B in FY22 to $23.6B in FY25 and FCF margin from 14.1% to 7.1%. Spending is still rising in 2026: the 10-Q's non-GAAP cash capex for the six months ended June 30, 2026 was $12,974M, higher than in the same period a year earlier. The trailing FCF yield is 4.6%. If consensus is right about FY26E, operating cash flow would likely rise with earnings, but the pack carries no 2026 cash-flow statement to confirm it, and the higher capex run-rate absorbs part of any gain. How the company uses its free cash flow is the subject of the Capital allocation section.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: ExxonMobil trades at a trailing P/E of 20.7x, a P/S of 1.8x and a trailing EV/EBITDA of 10.5x. The vendor's NTM P/E of 13.7x sits close to the price over FY26E EPS of $11.80, so we treat it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS the multiple is ~14.9x. The FY27E multiple is the higher of the two because consensus EPS falls to $10.84 in FY27E. The trailing multiple sits above both because consensus expects 2026 earnings far above trailing earnings, so it shows the price looking past trailing results more than what the market pays for normal ones. The pack has no EBITDA line of its own, so we cite the vendor's EV/EBITDA but do not build on it. No peer multiples were captured, so we do not benchmark ExxonMobil against other integrated majors. The Street's targets run from $142.00 to $200.00, with a consensus of $171.91 and a median of $173.50; 10 of 25 analysts rate the shares Buy, 15 Hold and none Sell. We do not adopt the consensus target as our Base, because the pack does not show the estimate or multiple behind it.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The supply disruption and the refining capacity reductions last through 2027, and consensus lifts FY27E toward the FY26E EPS of $11.80. A year out the market expects no further fade, so it pays the Base's multiple on that higher figure, which gives $175.82, close to the 52-week high of $176.41. We assume no re-rating above the multiple the market pays today for FY27E.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus proves right: a year out, FY27E EPS of $10.84 is the current-year figure, with margins eased from their 2026 level but the disruption not fully unwound. The pack holds no estimate beyond FY27E, so we assume no further fall is priced, and the market pays a year out the ~14.9x it pays today for the same estimate. That gives $161.52, roughly today's price by construction; the commentary argues the multiple.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Refining margins and gas prices return to their 10-year ranges within the year, and earnings fall back to FY25's $6.70. With nothing left to unwind, the market pays more per dollar of earnings than the Base does, and the shares return to the 52-week low of $110.39, a price they traded at within the past year. That is a higher multiple of FY25 EPS than the Base's but below the trailing P/E, so the whole fall comes from earnings. We do not deepen it for net debt, because a P/E-based price is already after finance costs.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base at 55%, the Bull at 25% and the Bear at 20%. The weighted fair value of $154.87 sits a little below the $161.23 price, the Bear about a third below it, and the page derives HOLD. The call is close, and it turns on the Base multiple. All three scenarios follow one rule: a year out, the market pays the lower current-year multiple only for earnings it expects to keep falling, and at least the FY27E multiple for earnings it does not. The case for the lower multiple in the Base is that FY27E still sits well above FY23–FY25 earnings and the 10-Q calls the gas disruption ongoing, so the market could still treat FY27E as elevated a year out. Applied to FY27E, that multiple is simply today's price moved down by the consensus EPS decline, and it derives SELL. We do not use it, for four reasons on the page. The Base itself has margins easing, so FY27E is less elevated than FY26E, which is when a cyclical earns a higher multiple. The 10-Q puts average crude prices within their range, so not all of the 2026 strength rests on out-of-range conditions. The Street has no Sell ratings, and its lowest target sits above the low end of our range. And the page's mechanical intrinsic read, a reverse DCF on trailing free cash flow and the growth five years of statements support, puts value above the price. Against that, the pack has no estimate beyond FY27E, so whether the market will still discount FY27E a year out is a judgment, not a finding. We give the Bull a quarter because its conditions are current in the latest 10-Q, but it needs consensus to raise an estimate it now expects to fall. We give the Bear a fifth because it needs both the refining and gas conditions to normalize within a year and earnings to give back the whole step-up. The label is close on the weights too: moving a few points from Bull to Bear derives SELL. The shares have risen sharply from the 52-week low and sit not far below the high. The page's recent closes hold in a narrow band near today's price, so the rise came earlier; no source dates or explains it.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The pack's revenue data carry ExxonMobil as a single consolidated segment, with FY25 revenue of $332.2B, while the company description and the 10-Q's cash-capex table name four segments. We use the consolidated revenue figure and do not assign revenue to individual lines. The four businesses are Upstream (crude oil and natural gas), Energy Products (fuels, aromatics and catalysts, plus licensing), Chemical Products (olefins, polyolefins and intermediates) and Specialty Products (lubricants, basestocks, waxes, synthetics, elastomers and resins). The 10-Q's cash-capex table shows where capital goes: of $6,787M of total cash capex in Q2'26, Upstream took $5,852M, Energy Products $527M, Chemical Products $307M, Specialty Products $11M and Other $90M. Upstream dominates investment, and management groups its growth around advantaged assets: Permian, Guyana and LNG.

moatFactors.name: Advantaged assets
moatFactors.body: ExxonMobil concentrates investment in what it calls advantaged assets, Permian, Guyana and LNG, and in advantaged projects it describes as delivering higher than average returns. Most of the company's cash capex goes to Upstream, which builds the resource base behind those assets. The advantage is real but cyclical: its value rises and falls with commodity prices.

moatFactors.name: Integration
moatFactors.body: The company spans exploration and production through fuels, chemicals and specialty products under the Exxon, Esso and Mobil brands. Holding both upstream and downstream businesses may soften the two-way commodity exposure the Risks section sets out, though the 2026 results show earnings can still move sharply.

moatFactors.name: Structural cost discipline
moatFactors.body: The 10-Q puts cumulative Structural Cost Savings at $16.3B relative to 2019, including $1.2B added in the six months ended June 30, 2026. Sustained cost reduction supports through-cycle margins. The measure is a company-defined non-GAAP figure set against a 2019 base, and the company notes the estimates may be revised if prior reductions prove unsustainable.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat narrow. Advantaged assets, integration and cost discipline are genuine, but the 10-K describes the business as fundamentally a commodity business, and returns follow prices and margins the company does not set. The long-run demand threats in the Risks section, and the early stage of the lower-emission ventures covered in Growth, limit how far the moat can widen. The net-zero ambitions for operated assets by 2050, and for integrated Upstream Permian Basin unconventional operated assets by 2035, frame a long transition rather than a near-term earnings driver.

points: Advantaged assets, Permian, Guyana and LNG, are the company's identified growth engines, and most of its cash capex goes to Upstream; the Business and moat section carries the capex split.

Consensus sees FY26E revenue of ~$411B, up {+ +24% +} on FY25. The pack does not split that rise into price and volume, and the 10-Q frames the period around supply disruptions and refining capacity reductions, so we treat part of it as cyclical; the Scenarios section weighs how much.
The 10-Q lists the integrated benefits the company plans from Denbury and Pioneer among its forward-looking statements; the pack gives no figure for them.
Structural cost savings are a lever on through-cycle earnings even without top-line growth; the moat section quantifies them.

Lower-emission ventures, including carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, lithium and lower-emission fuels, are long-term options that the company says depend on policy support and technological progress, so we give them no value in the scenarios.

management.leadership: The pack includes no executive-officer roster, so we do not name individual managers. The 2026 proxy statement, filed in April 2026, describes a largely refreshed board: nearly 70% of directors have joined since 2021, and the average independent-director tenure is 4.6 years, which the company presents as balancing continuity with fresh perspective. The board lists capital discipline, portfolio optimization, risk management and safety, long-cycle investment stewardship and shareholder engagement as its oversight priorities. A proxy footnote claims leading earnings ex. identified items and cash-flow-from-operations growth versus each of the other IOCs from 2019 to 2025; if accurate, that points to sound execution through a volatile cycle, but it is the company's own comparison.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation favors shareholder returns and Upstream investment, and in the last two years returns have outrun free cash flow. In FY25 the company paid $17.2B in dividends, which the proxy says ranked second among all S&P 500 companies per Bloomberg data. It also repurchased $20.3B of stock. Together those payouts exceeded FY25 free cash flow, as they did in FY24; from FY21 through FY23 free cash flow covered both. The shortfall shows up on the balance sheet, where cash fell and net debt rose, as the Financials section sets out. Dividends alone sit within free cash flow, so the buyback is the flexible part of the program, while capex, the other call on cash, keeps rising as the Cash flow commentary shows. In our view the current buyback pace depends on the 2026 earnings strength lasting: if margins revert, either buybacks slow or net debt keeps rising. We would expect the buyback to give way first, though the company has not said so.
management.governance: Governance scores well on independence. The 2026 proxy statement, filed in April 2026, reports that 12 of 13 directors are independent, that 100% of the Audit, Compensation, Nominating and Governance, and Environment, Safety and Public Policy committee members are independent, and that a Lead Independent Director holds defined authorities. Shareholders were asked to ratify PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP as auditor for 2026 and to cast an advisory say-on-pay vote. The proxy also asked them to approve redomiciling the company from New Jersey to Texas, its headquarters state; the board said shareholder rights remain largely comparable and that it is not adopting elective Texas provisions that weaken them. The pack does not report the vote results. Related-person transactions fall under written guidelines overseen by the Nominating and Governance Committee. The pack carries no executive-pay amounts or insider-ownership figures, so we do not assess them.

idiosyncratic: Faster normalization. The refining and gas conditions behind the 2026 step-up can reverse within a year, and consensus leaves little room for that, as the Financials section shows. With the shares near their 52-week high, a faster fade would reach the price quickly; the Bear case prices a full unwind.

Two-way commodity exposure. The 10-K states that a material decline in oil or natural gas prices could have a material adverse effect, especially in Upstream, while a material increase could hurt Energy Products, Chemical Products and Specialty Products. Integration softens this but does not remove it, so we treat ExxonMobil as a cyclical holding, not a defensive one.

Chemical weakness. The 10-Q says chemical margins improved but remained below the bottom of their 10-year range, with regional supply constraints affecting product availability, particularly in Asia; a longer stretch at those levels would weigh on the non-Upstream businesses.
risks.systemic: ExxonMobil faces the broad forces that move every oil, gas and petrochemical producer. Demand tracks global economic activity, so recessions or slow growth reduce results directly, per the 10-K. Supply depends on OPEC and OPEC+ production quotas, government policies that restrict or expand oil and gas production, and wars or other disruptions to transport routes. Interest rates, inflation and currency movements affect costs and demand. Over the long run, efficiency gains, alternative energy and changing consumer preferences could erode demand for the company's core products. None of these is specific to ExxonMobil, but its earnings follow commodity prices and margins, so they reach its results directly.

body: Our recommendation is HOLD, with a target range of $140 to $163 around a Base implied price of $161.52. ExxonMobil is a well-governed, cash-generative major whose 2026 earnings step-up the price already reflects, and it now carries net debt of $32.9B while paying out more than its free cash flow. The label rests on valuing FY27E a year out at the multiple the market pays for it today, which the Scenarios section argues from both sides.

On unchanged scenarios the label moves with the price: just above the top of our range the page derives SELL, and at the bottom of the range it derives BUY. Away from price, we would move to SELL if consensus cuts FY27E while the refining and gas conditions ease, because that is the case for the lower current-year multiple.
